vignette:
He is eighteen, a South Eastern Asian young man who introduces himself first as a photographer, as if that identity might steady the rest of the story. He still carries his camera most days, the strap wrapped twice around his wrist, though he says he rarely takes pictures the way he used to. Before the fighting, he had been the kind of boy who noticed light on puddles, smoke rising from food stalls, his friends laughing in alleyways at dusk. He remembers wanting to capture ordinary life before it changed, though at the time he did not know how much change was coming.

The combat enters his life quickly and then seems to swallow everything around it. He is still a teenager when armed conflict reaches his neighborhood. At first he photographs damaged buildings and men moving through the streets with rifles, telling himself he is documenting history. Adults praise his courage, and he clings to that. The camera gives him a role and a way to stand close to danger without admitting fear. Then one afternoon he follows a group of fighters and civilians sheltering near a market. He remembers the heat, the metallic smell in the air, and how sharply he can still see a red plastic bag caught on broken concrete. There is incoming fire, then a blast close enough to throw him sideways. For a few seconds he cannot hear anything except a high ringing. When the sound returns, it comes back as screaming.

He sees bodies where people had been standing moments before. A man he had photographed earlier is on the ground, reaching weakly toward nothing. A younger boy, maybe not much younger than he is, lies motionless under dust and shattered fruit crates. He remembers trying to lift his camera and finding that his hands do not work properly. Later he is ashamed that part of him keeps noticing frames, angles, light falling across blood. He takes some photographs automatically and then feels sick about it for months. He tells himself that if he had not gone there, if he had warned someone, if he had been faster, maybe one person would have lived. He knows other people tell him this is not true, but the thought returns with the force of fact.

Since then, the event does not stay in the past. It arrives uninvited in fragments so vivid that he feels pulled back into the market. A motorcycle backfiring in traffic makes his whole body jerk before he can think. The pop of fireworks or construction noise sends him searching for cover, heart pounding, eyes scanning exits and rooftops. He avoids crowded markets now, especially in the afternoon light that resembles that day. If he must go, he keeps moving, shoulders tense, studying faces and bags and windows. He says he is "just being careful," but he is exhausted by how hard he has to work to feel minimally safe.

Sleep offers little relief. He stays up editing old photographs or scrolling through images he cannot delete, then dreads closing his eyes. When he does sleep, he wakes sweaty and disoriented, sometimes already halfway out of bed, convinced for a moment that the room is filling with smoke. His family has heard him shout in the night. In the morning he often feels ashamed and irritable, snapping at people for small things and then withdrawing. He used to spend hours wandering with his camera, waiting patiently for the right moment. Now he startles at movement in his peripheral vision and loses concentration mid-shot. He goes out intending to photograph street scenes but comes home with empty memory cards because he cannot tolerate standing still in public.

What troubles him almost as much as fear is how cut off he has become. Friends ask him to meet, but he declines or leaves early, overwhelmed by noise and by the effort of pretending to be normal. He is single, and when people his age talk about the future, romance, work, he feels older than them and strangely absent from his own life. He says he used to feel emotion through photographs; now he mostly feels numb, except when anger or terror breaks through. Sometimes he studies his old images and barely recognizes the person who made them. At other times he fixates on tiny details from the blast-the red bag, the ringing, the boy under the crates-as if remembering them perfectly might somehow honor the dead or prevent forgetting from becoming another betrayal.

Even now, with the worst of the fighting no longer around him in the same way, his body behaves as though the attack could happen again at any moment. He sits near doors, watches people's hands, and maps escape routes without meaning to. He tells himself he should be stronger, that other people survived worse, yet he is living inside a constant readiness he never chose. Photography remains the thread connecting who he was to who he is; he still reaches for the camera when words fail. But what once helped him witness the world now also pulls him back toward the moments he cannot stop reliving.
